justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable, mean-reverting asset or indicator that was trading near 97 at the time of the forecast. For the one-day horizon, the estimate of 97.1 essentially embeds very little expected movement, consistent with typical short-term drift assumptions where momentum is modest and no major catalysts were immediately anticipated. The one-week estimate of 97.5 nudges slightly higher, reflecting a mild upward bias that could stem from prevailing trend conditions or a modest positive carry dynamic. The one-month estimate of 98.2 continues that gentle drift, suggesting I saw a shallow but persistent upward tendency over the medium term, perhaps anchored by fundamental or macro conditions that were supportive but not dramatically so.

The confidence interval widths widen appropriately as the horizon extends, driven by the compounding of daily volatility over time. At one day, the 90% interval of roughly 95.5 to 98.7 reflects near-term realized volatility being relatively contained — a spread of about 3.2 points. By one week, the interval opens to around 7 points, incorporating the square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty plus potential for intra-week news flow. At one month, the roughly 14.5-point wide interval acknowledges that a full month introduces substantial room for macro surprises, data releases, and shifts in sentiment that are simply impossible to predict with precision at the time of the forecast.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include sudden shifts in central bank policy communication, unexpected geopolitical events, or a liquidity shock that triggers outsized moves disconnected from fundamentals. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected data print or a risk-on sentiment surge could push the one-month outcome well above 105.5. On the downside, a financial stress event, credit scare, or sharp reversal in correlated markets could easily breach the 91.0 lower bound.

It is also worth acknowledging model risk itself as a source of tail exposure. The intervals were likely constructed assuming something close to normally distributed returns, which historically underestimates the frequency and magnitude of true tail events. Fat tails, regime changes, and sudden correlation breakdowns all represent structural reasons why real-world outcomes can exceed even well-calibrated 90% intervals more than 10% of the time.
